F joins B, C and D and scores 2.50, E, the only way out of A, scores 1.33, and G, which only touches D, scores 0." width="100%"} Betweenness measures how often a node lies on shortest paths, i.e. how much it acts as a broker or bridge. In a bipartite graph, any path between two nodes on the same side must pass through nodes on the other side, so brokerage is naturally a property of one partition relative to the other. This method scores the nodes of the chosen partition by how often they sit *between* nodes, counting shortest paths that start at nodes of the opposite partition. Concretely, it runs a shortest-path search (Brandes' algorithm, hop counts, edge weights ignored) from every node in the opposite partition to all nodes it can reach. Each node in the chosen partition collects the fraction of those shortest paths that pass through it (endpoints don't count). The totals are then multiplied by `2 / (m * (m - 1))`, where `m` is the size of the opposite partition (no scaling when `m < 2`). Because paths to every reachable node are counted, not only to the opposite partition, the scores are not limited to `[0, 1]`; compare them with each other rather than against a fixed scale. Typical uses include finding: - events or venues that connect otherwise separate groups of people - diseases that link distinct clusters of genes - products that bridge different customer segments Only nodes in the chosen partition are scored, and a node with a single neighbor always scores `0.0`. The method performs one search per node in the opposite partition, so its cost grows roughly with the size of that partition times the number of edges. On directed graphs edge direction is ignored, so shortest paths are those of the underlying undirected graph. The whole graph is used and the current selection is ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [which]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which partition to compute centrality for: `0` (default) or `1`. Partitions are numbered as in `bipartite_sets()`: in each connected component, partition `0` is the side that contains the component's lowest node ID. The shortest paths are started from the nodes of the *other* partition. Any other value raises an error. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node DataFrame column the scores are written to. If `None` (default), the column is named `"bipartite_betweenness_centrality"`. Only nodes in the chosen partition are written: if the column is new, the other nodes get null values; if it already exists, their existing values are kept. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `False` (default), returns the graph itself so calls can be chained, and records the computation so it is listed by `describe()`. If `True`, returns the scores as a dictionary instead, without writing anything to the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping each node ID in the chosen partition to its betweenness score. These are scaled sums of path fractions, so they are not limited to the range `0` to `1`. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): the graph itself, for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not bipartite, or if `which=` is not `0` or `1`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this people-film network the films are partition `1`. "Film2" links "Bob", "Cal", and "Dee", so it lies on the most shortest paths and gets the top score. "Film3" is attached only to "Cal", so nothing passes through it and it scores `0.0`: ::: {#fd94b614 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Cal", "Dee", "Film1", "Film2", "Film3"]) .add_edges( [ ("Ann", "Film1"), ("Bob", "Film1"), ("Bob", "Film2"), ("Cal", "Film2"), ("Cal", "Film3"), ("Dee", "Film2"), ] ) ) scores = graph.bipartite_betweenness_centrality(which=1, return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): round(score, 3) for nid, score in sorted(scores.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'Film1': 1.333, 'Film2': 2.5, 'Film3': 0.0} ``` ::: ::: Scoring the people instead (`which=0`) shows the brokers on that side: "Bob" and "Cal" each join two films, while "Ann" and "Dee" have a single film each and score `0.0`. Here the scores are stored under a custom column name and read back from the node DataFrame: ::: {#141caac2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( graph .bipartite_betweenness_centrality(which=0, attr_name="brokerage") .get_node_df() .select(["label", "brokerage"]) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
